e.etymology: A spelling of Joy, the English word, which came from Old French joie. Joye is also a variant of the surname Joy.
A spelling of Jarrett, an English surname that is a variant of Garrett, from the Germanic names Gerard, spear plus hardy, and Gerald, spear plus rule.
A short form of Julius and Julian for men and of Julia and Julie for women, all from the Roman family name Julius. In German, Jule is a pet form of Julia.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Juul, the e-cigarette brand

e.etymology: From the English surname, a nickname that told a younger man from an older relative with the same name. Young is also a common romanized element in Korean given names.
A spelling of Beverly, from the Yorkshire town of Beverley, whose Old English name means beaver stream. It was a surname and a man's name before it became a girl's name around 1900.
The Spanish feminine of Felipe, or Philip, from Greek Philippos, joining philos, loving, and hippos, horse. Its English counterpart is Philippa.
From Late Latin Clemens, merciful, the name of early saints and popes. It is the German and Dutch form of Clement and also an English surname.
namesakes: Samuel Clemens (real name of Mark Twain)
Roger Clemens (seven-time Cy Young Award pitcher)

e.etymology: A spelling of Dalton, an English place name and surname from Old English dael, valley, plus tun, settlement.
A spelling of Keenan, from the Irish surname Ó Cianáin, descendant of Cianán, a pet form of cian, ancient or enduring. Comedian Keenen Ivory Wayans made this spelling familiar around 1990.
namesakes: Keenen Ivory Wayans (creator of In Living Color)

assoc.t: Keenen Ivory Wayans, creator of In Living Color

e.etymology: A spelling of Kiefer, a German surname meaning either pine tree or, as a form of Küfer, barrel maker. Actor Kiefer Sutherland brought it into use around 1990.
A spelling of Adolf, from the Old High German name Athalwolf, joining adal, noble, and wolf.
namesakes: Adolph Coors (founder of the Coors brewery)
e.note: Bound to Adolf Hitler since the 1930s; the name has been all but abandoned in the US and Europe.

e.etymology: A variant of Gina, itself a short form of Georgina and Regina, or a short form of Genevieve.
namesakes: Gena Rowlands (actress in A Woman Under the Influence and The Notebook)

e.etymology: A French feminine form of Claude, from the Roman family name Claudius, which comes from Latin claudus, lame. Colette's Claudine novels of the early 1900s made it fashionable in France.
An American name joining the popular prefix La- to the ending of Patrice and Beatrice.
A feminine form of Daniel made with the Spanish-style ending -ita. Daniel is Hebrew for God is my judge.
A spelling of Ruby, the gem name, from Latin rubeus, red. Jewel names came into fashion in the late 1800s.
A spelling of Lindsay, a Scottish surname and clan name taken from Lindsey in Lincolnshire, Old English for the island of Lind, the old name of Lincoln.
A spelling of Laurinda, an elaboration of Laura, from Latin laurus, laurel.
A spelling of Dwayne or Duane, from the Irish surname Ó Dubháin, descendant of Dubhán, a pet form of dubh, dark or black.
A spelling of Keisha, an African-American coinage of the 1960s and 1970s that may draw on Keziah, the Biblical name meaning cassia.
An American coinage that puts Ka- in front of the -nisha ending of Tanisha and Shanisha, or stretches Keisha by a syllable.
A clipping of Alicia, Felicia and other names that end in the same sound.
A spelling of Roderick, from a Germanic name joining the words for fame and ruler. Its Latin form Rodericus was borne by the last Visigothic king of Spain.
From the Scottish surname Mac Artair, son of Arthur. Use as a first name peaked in 1942, when General Douglas MacArthur was an American war hero.

assoc.t: General Douglas MacArthur of World War II

e.etymology: A pet name that families used for Nora and other names, sometimes registered as a given name in its own right.
From the surname meaning son of Mathew. Matthew comes from Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of God. Mathews is also a given name among the Christians of Kerala in India.
A spelling of Ilya, the Russian form of Elijah, from Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is the Lord. American use peaked in 1966, when Illya Kuryakin was the Russian agent on The Man from U.N.C.L.E.
namesakes: Illya Kuryakin (Russian agent in The Man from U.N.C.L.E.)

e.etymology: A nickname, usually short for Captain, that was sometimes registered as a given name in the late 1800s.

assoc.t: cap, slang for a lie, as in no cap; also a hat

e.etymology: A spelling of Tammy, a pet form of Tamsin and Tamara that became a hit on its own after the 1957 film Tammy and the Bachelor.
A variant of the Manx surname Kermode, the Isle of Man form of Mac Diarmata, son of Dermot. Americans took it up after Kermit Roosevelt, a son of President Theodore Roosevelt.
namesakes: Kermit the Frog (host of The Muppet Show)
Kermit Roosevelt (explorer and son of Theodore Roosevelt)

assoc.t: Kermit the Frog of the Muppets

e.note: Kermit the Frog owns this name for most Americans, so expect frog jokes.

e.etymology: A pet form of Barnabas, Barnaby, Bernard and Barnett, and also an English surname taken from a place name.
namesakes: Barney Fife (bumbling deputy on The Andy Griffith Show)
Barney Rubble (Fred's neighbor on The Flintstones)
Barney Stinson (character on How I Met Your Mother)

assoc.t: Barney, the purple dinosaur of children's TV
Barney Fife of The Andy Griffith Show

e.note: Best known from Barney the purple dinosaur and bumbling Barney Fife, so expect teasing.

e.etymology: From Old French Mahaut, the medieval spoken form of Matilda, a Germanic name joining the words for might and battle. Tennyson's 1855 poem Maud brought it back into fashion.
